input_signals.name: Intangible Accrual Capitalization
input_signals.hypothesis: Intangible-asset growth accompanied by high accruals predicts lower future returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Intangible growth may represent productive investment, but high accruals suggest that reported earnings are not being converted into cash. This combination raises the risk of deferred expense recognition, impairment, or disappointment in expected intangible-asset payoffs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( intan, 1 ), at ) ), rank( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Noncapex Operating-Accrual Expansion
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(GROWTH(at, 1), RATIO(capx, at))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms whose asset growth exceeds real capital spending and is accompanied by operating working-capital accrual buildup earn lower subsequent returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This separates asset expansion not explained by capex from productive investment, then asks whether that residual expansion is tied to accounting accrual accounts. The mechanism is not simply “high asset growth and high accruals,” but specifically balance-sheet growth that appears to come through operating accrual accumulation rather than real capital formation.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( growth( at, 1 ), ratio( capx, at ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( sub( delta( act, 1 ), delta( che, 1 ) ), sub( delta( lct, 1 ), delta( dlc, 1 ) ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Accrual-Financed Capex Strain
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, at)), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), NEG(RATIO(oancf, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: High capex predicts especially low returns when reported earnings rely on accruals and operating cash flow is weak.
input_signals.reasoning: This aligns with the investment anomaly by treating aggressive capex as bad, but refines it by identifying firms where the spending is not well supported by cash generation. Unlike the prior indicator version, the signal preserves cross-sectional variation and makes the short-leg mechanism interpretable as low accrual strain rather than a zero-valued mixture.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( capx, at ) ), sumrank( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ), neg( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity Noninventory Accrual Build
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(ppegt, 1), at)), RANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), 1), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross PPE expansion accompanied by growth in noncash, noninventory current assets predicts lower subsequent returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This moves away from decomposing the full operating cycle into inventory, receivables, and payables and instead isolates current-asset accrual buildup outside inventory. Capacity expansion is more suspect when it coincides with receivables, prepaids, or other noncash current assets rather than cash-realized demand.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( ppegt, 1 ), at ) ), rank( ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), invt ), 1 ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Goodwill Expense Shield
input_signals.hypothesis: Goodwill growth accompanied by low depreciation and amortization expense predicts lower future returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This avoids another permutation of non-goodwill intangible growth and the recycled aoloch drain leg. Goodwill expansion reflects acquisition premia that are not systematically amortized, and low D&A intensity suggests limited expense recognition against the newly capitalized acquisition value.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( gdwl, 1 ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( dpc, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Depreciated-Capacity Cash Earnings
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ppegt, ppent), ppegt)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms with highly depreciated tangible assets and cash-backed earnings earn higher subsequent returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This addresses the prior aged-capacity failure by changing the economic interpretation: an old PPE base is not necessarily bearish if earnings are supported by cash rather than accruals. The signal targets conservative book asset values and proven cash productivity, distinguishing productive legacy capacity from accrual-supported underinvestment.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ppegt, ppent ), ppegt ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Legacy Capacity Cash Productivity
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms with highly depreciated tangible assets that still generate strong operating cash flow earn higher subsequent returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not another rank re-encoding of low Sloan accruals; it directly asks whether old productive assets are still producing cash. A high accumulated-depreciation share can indicate conservative book values, and strong operating cash flow validates that the legacy asset base remains economically productive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ppegt, ppent ), ppegt ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity Operating-Liability Gap
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(ppegt, 1), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), 1), DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1)), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross PPE expansion accompanied by noninventory current-asset buildup not financed by operating current liabilities predicts lower future returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This addresses the prior capacity-noninventory conflict by separating healthy operating-liability financing from unfinanced current-asset accrual growth. Capacity expansion is more suspect when receivables, prepaids, or other noninventory current assets rise without matching supplier or accrued-liability support.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( ppegt, 1 ), at ) ), rank( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), invt ), 1 ), delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Unpaid Goodwill Accrual Premium
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(DELTA(gdwl, 1), at), RATIO(aqc, at))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Goodwill growth that exceeds reported acquisition cash outlays and is accompanied by accrual-heavy earnings predicts lower future returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This avoids the mechanically unsound goodwill-amortization premise by focusing on purchase-accounting intensity rather than D&A expense. Goodwill growth not matched by acquisition cash outflow can reflect stock-funded or noncash purchased growth, and high accruals suggest the reported benefits are not yet cash-validated.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( ratio( delta( gdwl, 1 ), at ), ratio( aqc, at ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Replacement-Cycle Low-Accrual Capex
input_signals.expression: MUL(MIN(RANK(RATIO(capx, at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ppegt, ppent), ppegt))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms replacing highly depreciated tangible assets while earnings are cash-backed earn higher subsequent returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This moves beyond old-assets-plus-cash-profitability by requiring actual replacement investment, not merely free cash flow from legacy capacity. Capex is more plausibly productive when it renews an aged asset base and reported earnings are not dependent on accruals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( min( rank( ratio( capx, at ) ), rank( ratio( sub( ppegt, ppent ), ppegt ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ) ) ) )
